title: Knowledge, attitudes, and practices of Jordanian mothers regarding acute gastroenteritis in children
content:
by Mahdi Ahmad Al-Shboul, Ali Mohammad Ahmad, Mohammad Tayseer Khashroom, Sara Najeh Almugheed, Abdulrahman Emad Alramahi, Zainab Maref Al-Zoubi, Dana Hasan Al-Essa, Razan Mathhar Namir

Purpose

This study aimed to evaluate the knowledge, attitudes, and reported practices of mothers living in Jordan regarding childhood acute gastroenteritis and to identify factors associated with poor knowledge, poor practice, lack of oral rehydration solution (ORS) awareness, and antibiotic use without medical consultation.

Methods

An analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 730 mothers living in Jordan using a structured Arabic-language questionnaire. Participants were recruited through paediatric hospital settings and social media using convenience sampling. Composite knowledge and practice scores were calculated, and four multivariable binary logistic-regression models were fitted to examine factors associated with the prespecified outcomes.

Results

The mean composite knowledge score was 15.73 ± 6.83 out of 28, corresponding to 56.18% of the maximum score, and 31.37% of participants were categorized as having poor knowledge. The mean composite practice score was 4.58 ± 1.71 out of 10, corresponding to 45.84% of the maximum score, and 61.23% were categorized as having poor practice. Overall, 54.52% identified three or fewer of the eight dehydration signs assessed, 59.59% were aware of ORS, and 3.15% selected ORS as their intended first action. Compared with residence in Central Jordan, residence in North Jordan was associated with higher adjusted odds of poor knowledge (aOR 2.18, 95% CI 1.38–3.45), poor practice (aOR 1.74, 95% CI 1.19–2.55), lack of ORS awareness (aOR 1.52, 95% CI 1.01–2.28), and antibiotic use without medical consultation (aOR 1.81, 95% CI 1.12–2.91). University-level education was associated with lower odds of poor knowledge and poor practice, while healthcare employment was associated with lower odds of poor practice and lack of ORS awareness.

Conclusion

Important gaps were identified in dehydration-sign recognition, ORS-related intended practices, and overall reported home-management practices. These findings support the development and evaluation of targeted caregiver-education initiatives emphasizing dehydration recognition, appropriate ORS use, safe medication practices, and timely care-seeking. Regional and educational differences may help identify groups requiring additional support; however, the observed associations should not be interpreted causally because of the cross-sectional design.
